note: '32% reduction with skeletons vs spinners' and '47% more likely to wait for content' are verbatim; the 30% is 'Progress indicators feel 30% shorter', not skeleton vs spinner
Says 'This progress indicator is used for full-page loads'; skeleton is only 'a placeholder for a loading page'. Contradicts skeleton for full-page loads
'skeleton loading screens improve perceived performance well' vs preloaders and progress bars; 'over blank screens' wording not seen
'go for a skeleton screen when content is being fetched, and layout context matters, such as feeds, dashboards'
'A skeleton should match the exact structure of the element you're loading in'
Cited URL 301s to /building-blocks/core/components/data-table/guidelines (200). 'If extra load time is expected to display information, use skeleton states instead of spinners.'

why: Carbon (after redirect), onething and PatternFly back skeleton-for-known-layout yes/yes. NN/g says full-page loads use a progress indicator, and the 30% in Steve Kinney is a different claim. The 200 ms show-delay has no source on any page, so capped at ok

note: 'Try to limit to 5 words (not counting articles or prepositions)' in the empty-state title guidance
'More content doesn't necessarily mean it's a better solution as there is a cognitive cost for having more content on the page.'
'They should be as specific as possible, answering the question What should the user do next?'
'State what the user can do with the product instead of what the product enables them to do.'
'pass the primary action first and secondary actions as empty buttons'
'Is content still loading? Did an error occur?' and 'Communicate system status to the user'

why: Six yes/yes: 5-word title limit (GitLab), extra content costs attention (Carbon), CTA specific (Salesforce), state what the user can do (PatternFly), primary action first (EUI), system status (NN/g). 'Explain in one sentence' has no source; minor

note: 'Rather than just quoting the error code, we should translate what it means to the user in plain language.' 504 example on page
'And use plain language.' in the error empty-state guidance, with Nielsen heuristic 9 (recognize, diagnose, recover from errors)
'Provide clear, descriptive error messages in plain language.' and 'Users often don't know what went wrong or how to fix it' (a problem statement, not a rule)
'In the error message explain what went wrong and how to fix it.'
'Explain what went wrong and how to fix it.'
'human-readable language ... not blaming the user'

why: Five yes/yes: plain language over raw codes (EUI, with its 504 example), use plain language (Carbon), what went wrong and how to fix it (GOV.UK, NHS), human-readable and not blaming the user (NN/g video). Abstracta is partly

note: 'Did an error occur?' and 'the user cannot know whether there truly are no details to display, whether an error has occurred, or whether the system is still processing'

'it's best to display a well-considered empty state, or no results view'; 'display the current search text ... to help people quickly catch any typos'. Search icon, title and subtitle not stated for the no-results view

why: Only NN/g backs the loading vs error vs genuinely-empty split yes/yes; Apple WWDC26 292 is partly (no-results view and search text). 'Stale' as a fourth state and 'never show empty until data arrives empty' have no source

note: 'Support Undo and Redo.'
'build in forgiveness: easy undo and confirmation for destructive actions'
'All changes are tracked with checkpoints, so you can easily undo the agent's work.' A product README describing a feature, not design guidance
'A mechanism is available for reviewing, confirming, and correcting information before finalizing the submission.' (legal and financial only)
'Use the summary list to summarise information, for example, a user's responses at the end of a form.' Change links allow edits; no 'before submission' wording seen
'the document should not change' after undo and redo in multiplayer editing. About multiplayer undo semantics, not offering undo instead of confirmation

why: Undo offered (NN/g, Apple WWDC26 250 with its 'confirmation for destructive actions') and confirm for legal and financial (WCAG 3.3.4) are all yes/yes. 'Name exactly what will happen' has no source; Cline and Figma describe product features, not guidance

note: 'Animation is one way to visually engage people while loading or processing is happening in the background.' About loading, not feedback for every action
'For frequent and minor actions, the response can be modest, whereas for infrequent and major actions, the response should be more substantial.' Also 'Offer informative feedback.'
Source id says checkbox-radio-design but the URL is the NN/g toggle-switch page: 'Toggle switches should take immediate effect and should not require the user to click Save or Submit'
'When a user updates their details, they expect to see this change in all parts of a service straightaway.'
'Why not use those loading times to add value to users?' Onboarding, not feedback on actions
'the feedback that cars provide must be clear, immediate, and understandable' is a car analogy for feedback on user actions

why: Shneiderman (modest for frequent or minor, substantial for major), the NN/g toggle (immediate effect, no Save) and GOV.UK (changes shown straightaway) are yes/yes. The inline, toast and page-message mechanisms have no source, so capped at ok

note: 'staggering the entrance of table content by 20 ms'; 'total time is still within 500 ms'. Stagger and total cap, not the hub-0013 durations

Focus state 'should appear pretty quickly (around 100-150ms)' and 'stroke or outline ... as opposed to relying on color change alone'. These are focus and press response times, not entrance or exit durations
'Give larger elements more time to animate than smaller elements.' Also staggered entry to soften large sets of items
'wind draws left to right to convey motion, whereas this Arabic character draws from right to left'. SF Symbols draw direction, not UI easing or durations
Listed as a common mistake: 'An ease-in easing for an enter animation when it's supposed to be ease-out'
'My advice: use ease-out for elements entering the screen. They arrive fast and settle gently, which feels responsive.'

why: Ease-out for entrances (Emil, Flavio) and longer for larger moves (Fluent) are yes/yes. The hub-0013 durations (150-250, 100-150, under 100 ms) and ease-in for exits have no external source; Carbon's 500 ms cap and NN/g's focus times are different things. Capped at ok

note: 'After pressing play, the video started playing with a visible close control'. A video stop control, not autoplay or reduced motion
'Carefully consider users with motion sensitivity when using motion to communicate contrast.' One line; no reduced-motion setting, fades or pause

Cited line is about captions, which does not back the motion rule. The same page says 'Designers should avoid complex language, autoplaying animations and videos, and flashing animations' (the never-flash clause)
'suppressing small idle animations, parallax or other motion effects, auto-playing videos'; 'Prefer Cross-Fade Transitions' replace the sliding transitions
'Implement prefers-reduced-motion media queries ... provide pause controls for auto-playing animations'
'Support users who prefer reduced motion by respecting the prefers-reduced-motion media feature.'

why: prefers-reduced-motion honoured (svg-animations-dev, modern-svg), cross-fade replacing slides (WWDC20), pause for auto-playing motion (modern-svg), avoid flashing (Carbon, whose cited line is captions). Four yes/yes; 'never flash' rests on one line

note: 'Motion brings clarity and character to Rovo's AI experiences.' Page has a 'Generative border' component; no line on showing generation status
Same line as P0042: animation engages during loading or background processing. Says nothing on competing animations
'Use motion to identify the next step, inform people of changes in the UI, and celebrate what they've accomplished.'
'Use display modes only when visual interaction improves the workflow.' About cards and carousels, not motion
'allows us to communicate with users in easily understood ways.' Generic; no point about competing animations
'By using too many animations, icons, images and text styles, it competes for somebody's attention.'

why: Motion explains a change (Fluent) and too many animations compete for attention (WWDC19 211) are yes/yes. Airbnb and Doherty are generic or loading-only; OpenAI is about display modes. 'Loop decoration' has no source

note: 'Include the most important points in the first two paragraphs on the page.' Also 'Cut unnecessary content.'
'reassurances were brought out visually in a lined or bulleted way' in a product-page experiment; nothing on cutting words
'brands presenting the most important or impactful information first'
'Structuring content into visually distinct groups with a clear hierarchy enables designers to align information with how people evaluate and process'
'Help your users orient themselves with headings and titles.'
'Keep to 3-8 items per carousel for readability.' True on the page, but it is about carousel item count, not writing copy

why: Most important first (NN/g 'first two paragraphs', Decision Lab), chunking (Laws of UX), headings (WWDC17 819) and 'cut unnecessary content' (NN/g) are yes/yes. GoodUI and the OpenAI carousel count are off target

note: Headline changed 'to focus more on the end-goal of the UX Academy program'. One A/B experiment, not a general rule
'Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.'
'they rely on beliefs and are limited by past experiences'. Mental models in general, not UI naming
Unreached: Meta returned HTTP 400 with an 'Error | Meta' page (123 chars of text). Article not readable; claim unverified
'use of word lists to maintain consistency throughout apps'
'A debugging engineer, a rejected applicant, and an auditor need three different artifacts' - AI explanation article; nothing on users needing domain language

why: Familiar words over jargon (NN/g), word lists for consistency (WWDC25 404) and end-goal headline (GoodUI 22, one experiment) are yes/yes. Meta on terminology is unreached; the mental-model and AI-explanation sources are weak

note: 'the median workspace creates just two dashboards, and adoption drops off quickly beyond that'; 'most go stale'
Dashboard genres 'typically oriented towards specific contexts, tasks, and users'. The 'not all possible data' wording was not seen
'If you find that the scope of your story needs to grow beyond two or three views, you can always create more dashboards.'
'Executive dashboards focus on business impact and high-level trends rather than technical details.' Executive-only, not the general one-audience rule

why: Two dashboards and drop-off beyond (Linear), two or three views and split when it grows (Tableau), specific audience and context (Bach) are yes/yes. Odown is executive-only and weak
